title: Boss: one runbook, every distro
summary: One install command for every distro, an upgrade report from the package database, and your own .deb.

steps.title: Portable runbooks
body: Your runbooks are written for Ubuntu, but the fleet also has Rocky, Arch, openSUSE and Alpine. Three tickets: an install
script that works on every family, an upgrade report from the real package database, and a package of your own team's
tool. All on a real Debian machine with `dpkg`, `apt` and `dpkg-deb`.

steps.title: One install command for every distro
prompt: `~/bin/pkg-install FILE PACKAGE...` that **prints** (does not run) the non-interactive install command for that os-release
file, as a provisioning script would run it:
Anything else: print `unsupported: TOOL` to stderr and exit 1. Try `~/bin/pkg-install ~/fleet/erp-01/os-release curl jq`.

checks.name: the right command for every fleet host
checks.cmd: declare -A c=([apt]="apt-get install -y" [dnf]="dnf install -y" [yum]="yum install -y" [zypper]="zypper --non-interactive install" [pacman]="pacman -S --noconfirm" [apk]="apk add --no-cache"); for f in ~/fleet/*/os-release; do t=$(bash "$DOJO_FILES/pkgmgr-ref.sh" "$f"); want="${c[$t]} curl jq"; got=$(~/bin/pkg-install "$f" curl jq 2>/dev/null); [ "$got" = "$want" ] || { echo "$f: got '$got', want '$want'"; exit 1; }; done
checks.fail: A host gets the wrong command (below).

checks.name: unknown distros fail cleanly
checks.cmd: f=$(mktemp); echo ID=plan9 > "$f"; out=$(~/bin/pkg-install "$f" curl 2>&1 >/dev/null); rc=$?; rm -f "$f"; test $rc = 1 && grep -q unsupported <<<"$out"
checks.fail: An unknown distro should print `unsupported: ...` to stderr and exit 1.

hints: `tool=$(~/bin/pkgmgr "$1"); shift`, then `"$@"` is the package list.
`case $tool in apt) echo "apt-get install -y $*" ;; dnf|yum) echo "$tool install -y $*" ;; ... esac`.
solution: # pkg-install FILE PACKAGE...: prints the install command for the distro described by FILE.
for f in ~/fleet/*/os-release; do ~/bin/pkg-install "$f" curl jq; done
steps.explain: Package **names** differ too (`python3-venv` vs `python3`, `build-essential` vs `@development-tools`), which is why real runbooks keep a small name map per family, or use Ansible's `package` module with per-family variables. Scripts use `apt-get` rather than `apt` because `apt`'s output is not stable for scripts.

steps.title: Which packages have updates?
prompt: `~/available.txt` is a package index from the mirror: `NAME VERSION` lines, some packages listed twice (two
suites). Compare it with what is **installed on this machine** (`dpkg-query`) and write `~/answers/upgrades.txt`:
one line `NAME INSTALLED -> NEWEST` for every installed package whose newest available version is greater, sorted by
name. Packages that are not installed are ignored. Compare versions only with `dpkg --compare-versions`.

checks.name: upgrades.txt is the upgrade report
checks.fail: The report does not match (diff below: `<` yours, `>` expected). Take the **greatest** available version per package, and skip packages `dpkg-query -W NAME` does not know.

hints: `dpkg-query -W -f='${Version}' NAME` prints the installed version, and fails for a package that is not installed.
For each name, keep the greatest version from the file: start with `best=`, and replace it when `dpkg --compare-versions "$v" gt "$best"`.
Loop over the unique names (`awk '{print $1}' ~/available.txt | sort -u`), and print `"$name $have -> $best"` when `dpkg --compare-versions "$best" gt "$have"`.
solution: awk '{print $1}' ~/available.txt | sort -u | while read -r name; do have=$(dpkg-query -W -f='${Version}' "$name" 2>/dev/null) || continue; best=; while read -r n v; do [ "$n" = "$name" ] || continue; if [ -z "$best" ] || dpkg --compare-versions "$v" gt "$best"; then best=$v; fi; done < ~/available.txt; if dpkg --compare-versions "$best" gt "$have"; then echo "$name $have -> $best"; fi; done > ~/answers/upgrades.txt
steps.explain: On a connected machine `apt list --upgradable` (after `apt update`) gives this report, and `unattended-upgrades` applies the security part automatically. Doing it by hand once shows what those tools rely on: the installed database, the repository index, and one comparison function. Never compare versions with `sort -V`: it gets `~` and epochs wrong.

steps.title: Package your team's tool as a .deb
prompt: The team's `shopctl` script is in `~/shopctl`. Copying it by hand to every server is how versions drift. Build a real
1. Lay out a package tree in `~/build/shopctl`: the script at `usr/local/bin/shopctl` (mode 755) and a
3. Install it with `sudo apt install ./...deb` and check that `dpkg -S /usr/local/bin/shopctl` names your package.
setup:
printf '#!/bin/sh
# shopctl: the shop team helper
echo "shopctl 1.2.0"
' > ~/shopctl/shopctl

checks.name: the .deb exists with the right control data
checks.cmd: f=~/build/shopctl_1.2.0-1_all.deb; test "$(dpkg-deb -f "$f" Package Version Architecture 2>/dev/null | tr "\n" " ")" = "Package: shopctl Version: 1.2.0-1 Architecture: all "
checks.fail: `dpkg-deb -f ~/build/shopctl_1.2.0-1_all.deb Package Version Architecture` should show `shopctl`, `1.2.0-1` and `all`.

checks.name: it depends on jq and curl
checks.cmd: d=$(dpkg-deb -f ~/build/shopctl_1.2.0-1_all.deb Depends 2>/dev/null); grep -qw jq <<<"$d" && grep -qw curl <<<"$d"
checks.fail: The package should have `Depends: jq, curl`.

checks.name: the files inside are owned by root
checks.fail: Inside the package, files should belong to `root/root`: build with `--root-owner-group`.

checks.name: shopctl is installed from the package
checks.fail: `dpkg -S /usr/local/bin/shopctl` should say `shopctl:` and running `shopctl` should work.

hints:
The control file: `printf 'Package: shopctl
Version: 1.2.0-1
Architecture: all
Maintainer: Shop Team <team@example.com>
Depends: jq, curl
Description: The shop team helper
' > ~/build/shopctl/DEBIAN/control`.
solution:
printf 'Package: shopctl
Version: 1.2.0-1
Architecture: all
Maintainer: Shop Team <team@example.com>
Depends: jq, curl
Description: The shop team helper
' > ~/build/shopctl/DEBIAN/control
explain: A package gives you versions, dependencies, clean removal (`apt remove shopctl`) and `dpkg -S` answers for free. Real
teams build packages in CI (with `nfpm` or `fpm` for .deb and .rpm from one config, or `debhelper` for Debian
proper), sign their repository, and serve it to their fleet. Containers changed where packages end up, not why
